body.text: Victorians will head to the polls on November 28 to decide who will form the next state government.
Labor and the Coalition's law and order policies will be under scrutiny today following three separate stabbing attacks in Melbourne over the weekend.
Follow our live coverage below:
Submit a comment or question
Live updates
Community safety and mental health in focus
Both Ben Carroll and Jess Wilson are likely to be asked about community safety today, following a violent weekend in Melbourne's CBD which saw multiple people stabbed in separate incidents.
On Saturday, a 24-year-old man was hospitalised after being stabbed by a man in what police say was an unprovoked attack.
Later that night night, a 21-year-old man from Narre Warren died from an alleged stabbing on La Trobe Street.
Two males, 17 and 18, have since been charged over the stabbing.
In a third separate event on Saturday night, a 33-year-old man sustained stab wounds and was left fighting for his life after an alleged altercation in a fast food restaurant carpark.
A 51-year-old man has since been arrested over that incident.
Both Labor and the Coalition have pledged to crack down harder on crime if re-elected, promising boosts to police numbers and tougher laws.
And we'll bring you the reaction from Ben Carroll and Jess Wilson, who are sure to be asked about the weekend of violence during their campaign stops today.

Bob Katter meets with voters in north-east Victoria
Queensland MP Bob Katter has hit the campaign trail north-east Victoria, visiting Tallangatta with Benambra independent Lachie McKeeman.
Katter spent Monday morning speaking with locals including several high school students who said they’d raced from the school grounds to the town’s local bakery to snap a picture with him.

The federal member for Kennedy earlier told ABC Goulburn Murray Breakfast he was visiting the region to support the independent candidates in a show of support for Independent Member for Indi Helen Haines who was allegedly attacked outside her Wangaratta electorate office in October.

"Helen Haines would be doing this job, except Helen has been cut down in the most terrible manner," Katter told ABC Goulburn Murray breakfast. "I was coming down at Helen's request originally to help her with the campaigns. "I am determined to get the independents' movement going throughout Australia. "The party system has failed us miserably."

Maverick MP comes to Victoria to help independent campaigns
While much of our focus goes towards the major parties with a chance of forming government, one man is calling for more focus on independents.
That man is Queensland MP Bob Katter.

The federal member for Kennedy says he is in the region to boost the independent movement in Victoria, which he says he discussed with MP Helen Haines before she was allegedly attacked outside her Wangaratta electorate office in October.

Premier pays tribute to Molly
While Jess Wilson tours Victoria's west, Ben Carroll is in Richmond, where he took a moment to pay tribute to Molly Meldrum.
He and his wife Fiona laid some flowers at a state of Meldrum (the one behind the Corner Hotel).

"Everyone, whether you had met Molly or in fact if you hadn't met Molly, you felt like he was a mate," Carroll said earlier today. "Molly Meldrum is an icon of the Australian music scene, he's one of the few people I know where you can have a hat that's as famous as the individual himself."

🎞️: All smiles on the campaign trail
While the election campaign has at times been fiery, it isn't total war between Labor and the Coalition.

Jess Wilson is campaigning today in Victoria's west for Liberal candidate for Wendouree Gav Ronan. But also at the early voting centre today was current Wendouree MP Juliana Addison, who had a much friendlier exchange than you might imagine.
After introducing Wilson to her husband who she had "heard a lot about", Addison shared a laugh with the opposition leader.
"How's things?" Addison says. "Good, how are you?" Wilson says. "Living my best life," she replies.

The nostalgia for traditional Victorian industries driving election campaigns
Nostalgia can be a delicate emotion, but potent for some voters.

In areas like Gippsland, which has seen major industries close and thousands of jobs lost over successive decades, political promises to revive traditional industries like timber and energy can resonate strongly.
The ABC's Madeleine Stuchbery covers the promises and what they mean for people in Victoria's east:
Wilson in full agreement on Molly Meldrum state funeral
Jess Wilson (being born in 1990, three years after Countdown ended) says her fondest memories of Molly Meldrum came from Hey Hey It's Saturday.
She says it's a tremendous loss for Victoria, and says she is in total agreement with the offer of a state funeral for Meldrum.

"My office and the premier's office have been speaking and during caretaker there is a convention that we agree whether or not there will be a state funeral," she says. "I've very happy to agree to a state funeral, Molly Meldrum is an icon of Victoria, he's an Australian legend and I think he deserves a state funeral."
"My office and the premier's office have been speaking and during caretaker there is a convention that we agree whether or not there will be a state funeral," she says.
"I've very happy to agree to a state funeral, Molly Meldrum is an icon of Victoria, he's an Australian legend and I think he deserves a state funeral."
Wilson on mental health
Wilson says its clear that mental health issues have played a role in some of the violent incidents seen over the past few months in Victoria, but says it would not excuse criminal behaviour.

"We need to make sure that we are looking at the mental health impacts here," Wilson says. "But it cannot be a place where we don't also ensure that we have serious consequences for breaking the law in this state."
"We need to make sure that we are looking at the mental health impacts here," Wilson says.
"But it cannot be a place where we don't also ensure that we have serious consequences for breaking the law in this state."

Jess Wilson vows to address crime before Christmas
The Liberal bus is in the seat of Ripon today in Victoria's west, with Jess Wilson joining local candidate Megan Read and Wendouree candidate Gav Ronan on the campaign trail.
She makes a strong pledge to address crime within her first 100 days in office if elected.

"We will recall the parliament this side of Christmas to pass tough new laws when it comes to bail and sentencing," Wilson says. "So that criminals understand that if you break the law in a Liberals-Nationals government, you will go to jail."
"We will recall the parliament this side of Christmas to pass tough new laws when it comes to bail and sentencing," Wilson says.
"So that criminals understand that if you break the law in a Liberals-Nationals government, you will go to jail."
Wilson calls the level of knife crime in Victoria "a disgrace" and says Victorians deserve a government that holds criminals to account.
Seats in focus: Murray Plains

Murray Plains was first contested at the 2014 election and covers territory once included in the now-abolished seats of Swan Hill and Rodney. These areas are National Party heartland and the seat’s retiring MP Peter Walsh, originally elected in 2002 as the member for Swan Hill, has been elected with margins of more than 20 per cent at all but his first contest.

The departure of Walsh, a long-serving member and former leader of the Victorian Nationals, leaves this seat vulnerable to One Nation, which received its best result at the 1999 election, more than 10 per cent of the primary vote, in the former seat of Rodney.
Greens will have to overcome Liberal preferences to snag inner Melbourne seats
An unpopular Labor government has buoyed the election chances of the Victorian Greens, with the party polling strongly.
But Ellen Sandell's party has to overcome a setback along the way: Liberal preferences.

Aside from retaining their current seats of Brunswick, Melbourne, and Richmond, the party wants to win back Prahran which it lost in a by-election in 2025. It also hopes to gain seats like Northcote, Pascoe Vale, Preston and Footscray from Labor, where its candidates fell narrowly short of wins in 2022.

Carroll comments on fourth reported stabbing in as many days
On the tails of three separate alleged stabbings on the weekend in Melbourne, Ben Carroll is asked about a fourth incident from this morning in Mickleham.
Police say four men gained entry to a home at 5.30am armed with machetes and a firearm. A 70-year-old man was stabbed while four other people including two children were home.
Investigators are still searching for offenders, who police believe fled in a stolen Toyota before crashing nearby and leaving the scene on foot.
Carroll gave his sympathies to the family, and says he would give Victoria Police all the powers they would need to tackle knife crime if re-elected.

"I re-affirmed this to the Chief Commissioner this morning. I will deliver the stop-and-search powers they need and deserve," Carroll says. "I will leave no stone unturned until we change the culture around knife crime, and that means starting with zero tolerance."

Mental health minister on asylums
Mental Health Minister Ingrid Stitt says the government will take its advice from experts on facilities like standalone mental health asylums.
Stitt says since the mental health royal commission delivered its recommendations in 2021, the government has doubled its funding in the sector.

"Clearly we are catching up, since 2021, from honestly had been decades of underinvestment in the mental health system in Victoria," Stitt says. "Now asylums were closed for good reason. They were not placed where people were getting the therapeutic care that they needed."

Carroll says he feels safe personally, but 'more work to do'
Carroll is asked about safety in Victoria in light of the weekend's violent incidents.
"I feel safe, but I know my focus is on making sure every Victorian feels safe," he says. "We've always got more work to do."
"I feel safe, but I know my focus is on making sure every Victorian feels safe," he says.
"We've always got more work to do."
He lists a range of policies targeting law and order he has enacted since becoming leader, including an increase in police powers and increased coverage of PSOs.
Carroll also discusses the work he's done in addressing homelessness.
"More money has gone into the Salvation Army since I've been premier," he says. "I appointed Victoria's first homelessness minister, $25 million to making sure people have a home."

Carroll makes MND pledge
Carroll turns from one Australian icon to another, from Molly Meldrum to Neale Daniher, who died in May after years of living with motor neurone disease (MND).
The premier says if re-elected, the government will make tackling MND a new priority and make it a notifiable disease.
Medical professionals who diagnose a patient with a notifiable diseases, such as cholera and hepatitis, are required by law to report it to the Department of Health.
Carroll says it would provide authorities with the data to facilitate "local solutions".

Premier Ben Carroll is speaking to media outside the MCG today, and confirms the family of Molly Meldrum have accepted his offer for a state funeral.

"All of our thoughts as Victorians and indeed Australians are with Molly Meldrum's family and his friends, and we know how wide that network was," Carroll says. "Even as a fellow North Melbourne supporter, I would have loved to have seen him see a premiership with the Saints."

What are parties doing on mental health?
Why don't the two major parties every focus on mental health in these cases instead of increasing police numbers and harsher laws. Why can't we have something like Broadmoor hospital? - Ekam
Why don't the two major parties every focus on mental health in these cases instead of increasing police numbers and harsher laws. Why can't we have something like Broadmoor hospital?
- Ekam
Hi Ekam,
There are two parts to your question, I'll do my best to tackle both.
Mental health is almost certainly a key policy issue that Labor and the Coalition have campaigned on.
The Coalition has promised to deliver a $50 million targeted mental health workforce fund, with $5 million dedicated to planning a youth mental health facility in Parkville.
Labor will fund $6 million dedicated youth mental health beds in Casey if elected, and $15.8 million to deliver supported housing for adults living with mental illness.
Then there's the second part of your question: Broadmoor Hospital, which is a specialist high-security psychiatric hospital.
The answer to that is we do have an equivalent: the high-security Thomas Embling mental health hospital in Fairfield.
The facility houses forensic and compulsory mental health patients.
But the facility has been the subject of several controversies lately, including staff shortages and an alleged sexual assault, as reported by the ABC's Rachel Eddie.
In it's May budget, the government pledged $125 million to open 40 new forensic mental health beds at Thomas Embling Hospital, but that funding remains up in the air with the election looming.
Seats in focus: Mulgrave
Since being recreated ahead of the 2002 election, Mulgrave has had just two representatives and both have been from the Labor Party.

Daniel Andrews was elected as the first member for recreated Mulgrave with a two-party preferred margin of more than 16 per cent. He was elected as leader of the Labor Party after its defeat at the 2010 election and led the party back to government at the following election. It was at this election that his margin in Mulgrave dropped to its lowest due to a redistribution which shifted the electorate northwards into more Liberal-friendly areas.

Outside of the 2014 election, the Liberal Party primary vote never exceeded 40 per cent. At the 2022 election, the Liberals were overtaken into second by local businessman Ian Cook running as an independent. Cook again came second in Mulgrave in the 2023 by-election caused by Andrews’s retirement.
Key Event
Melbourne Lord Mayor says mental health asylums should be considered
Following the weekend of violent incidents, Melbourne Lord Mayor Nick Reece spoke with 774 ABC Melbourne to discuss his concerns over links between mental health and violent crime.

"Melbourne is a great city. It's a safe city as well compared to other cities like ours around the world. In fact, our crime rate has come down 5.9 per cent in the central city over the last 12 months, and that's been a lot of work we've been doing at the city level and at the state," he said.
"But now these shocking incidents come along and you know it's just derailing all our efforts. We really want to have a focus on the mental health moment and how that's presenting on our streets."

Reece said the city would bring forward a planned mental health roundtable which will feature clinicians at the Royal Melbourne Hospital, representatives of the Victorian Government and Professor Patrick McGorry.
Reece said asylums for people experiencing serious mental health issues should be explored, and that experts such as Professor McGorry said deinstitutionalisation had not worked.

"That is definitely one of the questions that I would like to ask. Should we consider bringing back asylums?" Reece said. "Not a return to the bad old days, but looking at long-term mental health facilities so people who need care can get it."
